name: Bridge between cycles

lead: In bodybuilding and physique-enhancement circles, a bridge is a period of reduced-intensity androgen use between full cycles, so the user does not drop entirely to a natural baseline. Practitioners say the aim is to hold on to muscle gained, which keeps the physique fuller between peaks.

The idea is discussed on gym and enhancement forums and overlaps with terms like "blast and cruise". It is a community practice: no clinical trials have studied it as a protocol, and the drugs involved are medically controlled.

paras: Forum descriptions are general: users move from a heavier phase to a maintenance-style phase rather than stopping, then return to a heavier phase later. Specific compounds, amounts and schedules are not given here.

Anabolic steroids can suppress natural testosterone production, and documented adverse effects include cholesterol and blood pressure changes, liver strain with some oral compounds, fertility effects and mood changes. They are controlled substances in many countries, and medical guidance, not forum advice, applies.

chain: Maintain a lower-intensity phase rather than stopping entirely
Hold more of the muscle built in the previous phase
angle.text: Users say staying on a reduced regimen between cycles preserves muscle they would otherwise lose, so appearance is less variable. This is the users' account and has not been tested as a protocol.

lead: A bridge between cycles is a term from bodybuilding and physique-enhancement communities for a lower-intensity period of androgen use placed between higher-intensity phases, usually called blasts or cycles. Practitioners describe it as a way to avoid a complete stop and the return to a natural baseline that follows, with the stated aim of holding on to more of the muscle built in the previous phase so that the physique stays fuller between peaks. It sits in the same family of ideas as cycling, "blast and cruise" and post-cycle therapy.

The practice concerns anabolic-androgenic steroids (AAS). Medical references describe these drugs as suppressing the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis, the signalling chain that drives the body's own testosterone production, and report that after a short course follow-up therapy usually restores normal production.[1] The Endocrine Society's 2014 scientific statement adds that after a lengthy course suppression can last months or years, and that some users do not regain normal testosterone levels.[2] Bridging is the community's answer to that stop-start pattern: staying on a reduced regimen rather than dropping to zero.

Bridging has not been tested as a regimen in a clinical trial. What exists is a literature on AAS use patterns, withdrawal and long-term health outcomes, which describes the context in which bridging is discussed. This article describes the concept in general terms; it does not give drugs, amounts or schedules.

paras: In practitioners' framing, a cycle is a defined period of heavier androgen use followed by a period off. Bridging replaces the "off" with a reduced-intensity phase: users move from the heavier phase to a maintenance-style phase rather than stopping, and later return to a heavier phase. The appearance logic is that muscle tissue gained during a heavy phase is more likely to be kept if the body remains under some androgen exposure, so that the user looks fuller between peaks and has a higher starting point for the next phase.

Bridging is discussed on gym and enhancement forums alongside several neighbouring terms. A full stop with recovery measures is often called post-cycle therapy; long periods at a lower level interrupted by short heavy phases are often called "blast and cruise"; and some users who follow a medically supervised testosterone replacement regimen describe that as their baseline between heavier phases. The Endocrine Society statement describes the broader pattern of users stacking several drugs and raising and lowering doses in cycles, noting that interactions between steroids and the other drugs commonly taken with them are poorly studied.[2]

Testosterone was discovered and synthesised in the 1930s, after which physicians began using androgens for a range of purposes.[1] Non-medical use followed in strength sports and bodybuilding, and surveys cited in the literature indicate that most non-medical users today are not competitive athletes but people who want a more muscular appearance.[1][2] One survey cited by Wikipedia found 78.4 percent of users were noncompetitive bodybuilders or non-athletes using the drugs for appearance, with a typical age around 25, and that information often comes from friends, handbooks, internet forums and fitness magazines.[1]

The language of cycles, stacks and bridges therefore comes largely from user-to-user transmission rather than from clinical practice. The Endocrine Society estimated that 2.9 to 4.0 million Americans have used an AAS at some point, with a typical onset age in the early twenties, and noted that use is common in Scandinavia, Brazil and the British Commonwealth and rare in East Asia.[2]

A related development has been the rise of testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) as a legitimate medical service. US testosterone use rose from 0.5 percent of men in 2002 to 3.2 percent in 2013 before falling to 1.7 percent in 2016, according to Wikipedia, and clinics offering TRT are part of the context in which "cruise" phases are discussed.[3] Sports regulators have drawn lines around this: the Nevada State Athletic Commission banned TRT for UFC fighters in 2014.[3]

Proponents of bridging say that muscle lost during a complete stop is hard to regain, that staying on a reduced regimen is easier on the body than repeated swings between suppression and recovery, and that it keeps strength, fullness and motivation steady. Some describe the approach as a compromise between continuous heavy use and repeated full cessation.

Clinicians and researchers describe the stop-start pattern differently. The Endocrine Society statement reports that after prolonged use suppression of the HPG axis may take months to years to resolve and can be incomplete, that users sometimes try clomiphene or hCG but the supporting evidence is limited to case reports with mixed results, and that no systematic treatment studies exist.[2] Researchers have also described a withdrawal syndrome with low mood and fatigue after stopping, which some users cite as a reason they do not stop fully.[2][4]

Kanayama and colleagues estimated that about 30 percent of AAS users develop a dependence syndrome, characterised by continued use despite harm, and argued that it resembles classical drug dependence with a withdrawal syndrome involving neuroendocrine and neurotransmitter systems.[4] In this literature, continuous use is discussed as a possible expression of dependence as well as a physique strategy; the two are not mutually exclusive in the accounts reviewed.

Forum descriptions of bridging stay at a general level: a heavier phase ends, a lower-intensity phase begins instead of a stop, and a heavier phase later resumes. Users often combine this with regular blood work, since the clinical monitoring literature emphasises cholesterol, blood pressure, hematocrit and hormone panels. Because testosterone-type drugs can raise hemoglobin, TRT guidance tells physicians to monitor hematocrit and PSA, and removal of blood by venipuncture is described as a treatment when hematocrit rises too high.[3] Specific compounds, amounts and schedules are not given here.

Medical references on anabolic steroids list adverse effects including adverse cholesterol changes, hypertension, left ventricular enlargement, liver damage with high doses of some oral agents, gynecomastia, testicular atrophy, reduced sperm count, and psychiatric effects such as aggression; adolescents may face premature growth plate closure.[1] The Endocrine Society statement describes cardiomyopathy, increased cardiac mass, dyslipidemia (lower HDL, higher LDL, especially with oral 17-alpha-alkylated steroids), coronary calcification, myocardial infarction, stroke and coagulation problems, and notes that some changes partly reverse after abstinence while fibrosis may be permanent.[2]

Suppression of LH and FSH can impair sperm production and cause infertility in men; the statement also describes hypomanic symptoms during use and depressive symptoms, sometimes with suicidality, during withdrawal, with mood disorders more common at very high doses.[2] A 2008 review of long-term consequences concluded that long-term supraphysiologic use may cause irreversible cardiovascular damage including atherosclerosis and cardiomyopathy, while evidence of lasting harm in other organ systems is more modest, and that systematic long-term data are lacking.[5]

Anabolic steroids are Schedule III in the US, Class C in the UK and Schedule IV in Canada, and black-market products may be counterfeit.[1] In February 2025 the FDA removed the boxed warning on prescription testosterone products after the TRAVERSE trial found no increased cardiovascular risk versus placebo in men with hypogonadism; that trial concerned medical replacement, not non-medical enhancement.[3]

No studies found. No trial has tested bridging as a regimen. Related research addresses broader categories: the Endocrine Society's 2014 scientific statement reviews adverse health consequences of performance-enhancing drugs and calls for observational studies and randomised trials of withdrawal treatments,[2] a 2009 review in Addiction examines AAS dependence,[4] and a 2008 review examines long-term psychiatric and medical consequences.[5]

In physique-enhancement circles, the bridge is part of a vocabulary for managing appearance over time, not just at a single peak. The practice is discussed as a way to avoid visible loss of size after a heavy phase. In wider looksmaxxing spaces, which weigh interventions by how they change facial and physical appearance, androgen use is often presented as one end of a spectrum that also includes natural training and nutrition; bridging belongs to the more advanced end of that discussion.

lore.intro: On gym and enhancement forums, bridging is described by users as a middle path between full cycles and continuous heavy use; research comments mainly on the stop-start pattern and on long-term effects.[2]
